query: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloys are promising bond-coat candidates because of their mechanical properties and elevated-temperature oxidation resistance. Earlier HVAF-M3 work identified 15–45 μm feedstock as optimal for high-quality coatings, but applying the same composition and size range with the HVAF-i7 torch yielded acceptable coating quality yet inadequate thickness. Separate studies of conventional MCrAlY bond coats using the M3 system reported a slight gain in deposition efficiency at higher particle velocity and nozzle-specific best spray distances of 300 and 350 mm. The design target is a sufficiently thick, adherent bond coat that retains coating integrity, minimal as-sprayed oxidation, and durability during high-temperature thermal-barrier service, including deposition within internal diameters as small as 120 mm. What single intervention could overcome the thickness limitation? State the hypothesized intervention and mechanism, predict the outcome relative to the 15–45 μm-feedstock baseline, define the deposition and service conditions under which it should remain effective, identify supporting evidence from the cited prior studies, and propose a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adjusting the HVAF‐i7 torch parameters to increase in-flight particle velocity—by optimizing the fuel/oxygen mix and adopting a nozzle-specific spray distance (around 300–350 mm)—will overcome the current thickness limitation by enhancing deposition efficiency without compromising oxidation resistance or adhesion.
generation.material_initial_state: Gas‐atomized FeCoNiCrAl powder with 15–45 μm particle size, which on the HVAF-M3 system produces high-quality coatings.
generation.intervention: Increase the in-flight particle velocity through combustion parameter adjustments and by tuning the spray distance to approximately 300–350 mm when using the HVAF-i7 torch.
generation.conditions: Deposition using the HVAF-i7 torch on substrates with internal diameters as small as 120 mm, under elevated-temperature service conditions suitable for thermal-barrier applications.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced kinetic energy of the sprayed particles leads to improved in-flight melting, deformation upon impact, and flattening of droplets, resulting in better interparticle bonding and a thicker, more adherent coating.
generation.mechanism: Higher particle velocity increases the impact energy on the substrate, which promotes better particle deformation and spreading. This, in turn, enhances the build-up of coating layers and improves the bonding, while the maintenance of controlled oxidation during rapid deposition preserves the coating's performance during high-temperature service.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified HVAF-i7 process will yield coatings with significantly improved thickness relative to the 15–45 μm baseline parameters (as seen with HVAF-M3), while maintaining minimal as-sprayed oxidation and excellent adherence suitable for internal diameters of 120 mm.
generation.baseline: Using 15–45 μm feedstock on HVAF-M3 yields high-quality coatings; however, the same parameters on HVAF-i7 result in acceptable quality but inadequate thickness.
generation.boundary: The intervention should remain effective under typical HVAF-i7 operating conditions, with spray distances around 300–350 mm and within the fuel/oxygen parameter window that avoids excessive oxidation. Its efficacy is assumed for the application range involving internal diameters of ~120 mm and high-temperature thermal-barrier service.
generation.uncertainty: There is some uncertainty regarding the precise tuning of the combustion parameters for the HVAF-i7 system and whether the optimized spray distance will universally translate to increased deposition thickness without inadvertently increasing oxidation or impacting adhesion. Further optimization may be needed for different substrate geometries.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a comparative study using the HVAF-i7 torch, where one set is sprayed using the baseline settings (15–45 μm feedstock, standard parameters) and a second set is sprayed with the adjusted parameters to achieve higher particle velocity by setting the spray distance to 300–350 mm and optimizing the fuel/oxygen ratio. Specimens should be deposited on substrates with internal diameters of 120 mm, and the coatings' thickness, oxidation state, and adhesion quality should be evaluated.
measurements: Oxidation level (via XRD and EDS analysis)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified HVAF-i7 parameters do not yield a statistically significant increase in coating thickness (relative improvement compared to the baseline) or if the coating exhibits increased oxidation or inferior adhesion compared to the baseline, the hypothesis would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: One of the most promising applications of FeNiCoCrMoAl-based high-entropy alloy is the fabrication of protective coatings. In this work, gas-atomized powder of FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 composition was deposited via high-velocity oxygen fuel spraying. It was shown that in-flight oxidation of the powder influences the coating’s phase composition and properties. Powder oxidation and phase transformations were studied under HVOF deposition, and during continuous heating and prolonged isothermal annealing at 800 °C. Optical and scanning electron microscopy observation, energy dispersive X-ray analysis, X-ray diffraction analysis, thermogravimetric analysis, differential thermal analysis, and microhardness tests were used for study. In a gas-atomized state, the powder consisted of BCC supersaturated solid solution. The high rate of heating and cooling and high oxygen concentration during spraying led to oxidation development prior to decomposition of the supersaturated solid solution. Depleted Al layers of BCC transferred to the FCC phase. One of the most promising applications of AlCoCrFeNi HEA is the fabrication of protective coatings [,]. HEA-based coatings, deposited on medium-carbon steel substrates, can considerably enhance the material performances, extend service life, and reduce product costs [,,]. Thick coatings with low porosity and a high level of adhesion can be produced via the high velocity fuel spraying (HVOF) technique [,]. HVOF is a combustion spray process in which a hydrocarbon fuel (kerosene, methane, propane, etc.) is ignited, mixing with oxygen to accelerate feedstock powder towards the substrate [,]. Depending on the particle’s size and location in the high-temperature flow, the particles undergo various transformations, such as melting, softening, spheroidization, precipitation, and surface or total oxidation, similar to those observed with the atmospheric plasma spraying (APS) method []. Lower particle temperatures than those achieved in plasma spraying and higher particle speeds result in lower in-flight particle oxidation and better coating densities.
